question: What is a binary tree and what are its traversal methods?
title: Binary Tree Traversals Java | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: A **binary tree** is a hierarchy where each **node** has at most **two children** (left and right). The four traversals: **inorder** (Left-Root-Right), **preorder** (Root-Left-Right), **postorder** (Left-Right-Root) are **DFS** (recursive/stack), and **level-order** is **BFS** (uses a queue). For a **BST**, inorder yields **sorted** order. All are **O(n)** time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know all four traversals, which are DFS vs BFS, and the inorder-sorted-BST property
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing up the Root position in pre/in/post, or not knowing level-order needs a queue
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State that inorder of a BST is sorted and that level-order is BFS via a queue

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Binary tree node: value + **left/right** children.
- **DFS**: preorder (Root first), inorder (Root middle), postorder (Root last).
- **BFS** = level-order, uses a **queue**.
- **Inorder of a BST = sorted** order.
- All traversals are **O(n)** time.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A binary tree is a hierarchical structure where each node holds a value and has at most two children, a left child and a right child. The topmost node is the root, and nodes with no children are leaves. There are four standard ways to traverse it. Three of them are depth-first, and they differ only in when you visit the root relative to its subtrees. Preorder visits the root first, then the left subtree, then the right. Inorder visits the left subtree, then the root, then the right. Postorder visits the left subtree, then the right, then the root last. The naming is a helpful mnemonic: pre, in, and post refer to where the root is visited, first, middle, or last. The fourth traversal is level-order, which is breadth-first. Instead of recursion, it uses a queue: you enqueue the root, then repeatedly dequeue a node, visit it, and enqueue its children, which processes the tree level by level from top to bottom. A really important property I'd mention is that an inorder traversal of a binary search tree produces the values in sorted ascending order, which is a direct consequence of the BST ordering rule and comes up constantly in interviews. All four traversals are O of n time, since each visits every node exactly once. The recursive DFS versions are concise, while level-order specifically needs a queue, and that distinction, recursion or stack gives DFS, queue gives BFS, is worth being crisp about.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A **binary search tree** orders nodes left-smaller / right-larger for **O(log n) search** of any value.

A **heap** is a **complete** binary tree satisfying only the **heap property** (parent <= children for a min-heap), giving **O(1) access to the min/max** but no efficient search for arbitrary values.

Heaps are usually stored in an **array**; BSTs use linked nodes. Use a BST for ordered search, a heap for priority queues.

question: What is a Binary Search Tree (BST) and what are its properties?
title: Binary Search Tree BST Java | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: A **Binary Search Tree (BST)** is a binary tree with an ordering rule: for **every** node, all values in its **left subtree are smaller** and all in its **right subtree are larger**. This makes **search, insert, delete O(h)** where `h` is the height - **O(log n)** when balanced, but **O(n)** if it degenerates into a linked list. An **inorder** traversal returns values **sorted**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you state the recursive (whole-subtree) ordering rule and the balance-dependent complexity
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only checking immediate children instead of the whole subtree, or ignoring the O(n) degenerate case
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Emphasize O(h): O(log n) balanced vs O(n) skewed, and inorder = sorted as the validity check

sections.title: What a Binary Search Tree Is
sections.content:
A **Binary Search Tree (BST)** adds an **ordering invariant** to a binary tree: for **every** node, **all** values in its **left subtree** are **less** than the node, and **all** values in its **right subtree** are **greater**. Critically, this applies to the **entire subtree**, not just the immediate children.

That ordering lets you discard half the tree at each step, so **search, insert, and delete** run in **O(h)**, where `h` is the tree height. When the tree is **balanced**, `h ~ log n`, giving **O(log n)**. But if you insert sorted data into a naive BST, it **degenerates** into a linked list with `h = n`, making operations **O(n)** - which is why self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) exist. An **inorder** traversal of a valid BST yields **sorted** values, the standard validity check.

sections.content:
blue|Ordering rule|~whole subtree|left subtree < node|right subtree > node|recursive invariant
emerald|Operations|~O(h) each|search, insert, delete|discard half each step|O(log n) if balanced
rose|Degenerate case|~sorted inserts|becomes a linked list|height = n|operations O(n)
amber|Validity|~inorder check|inorder = sorted|use bounds in recursion|balance with AVL/red-black

sections.title: BST Search and Validity
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Checking only direct children**: validity needs the **whole subtree** within bounds - pass `(low, high)` down.
- **Ignoring degeneration**: sorted inserts make a naive BST O(n); mention balancing.
- **Assuming O(log n) always**: it's **O(h)**; only balanced trees give log n.
- **Forgetting inorder = sorted**: the simplest validity check.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- BST rule: **entire** left subtree < node < **entire** right subtree.
- Search/insert/delete are **O(h)**.
- **Balanced** -> O(log n); **skewed** -> O(n).
- **Inorder traversal = sorted** values.
- Self-balancing (AVL, red-black) guarantees O(log n).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A binary search tree is a binary tree with an ordering invariant. For every node, all the values in its left subtree are smaller than the node, and all the values in its right subtree are larger. The crucial word there is every, and it applies to the whole subtree, not just the immediate left and right children. A common mistake when validating a BST is to only compare a node with its direct children, which misses violations deeper down. The correct check passes a valid range down the recursion: each node must fall within a low and high bound, and you tighten that bound as you go left or right. The payoff of the ordering rule is efficiency. Because I can decide at each node whether to go left or right, search, insert, and delete all run in O of h, where h is the height of the tree. When the tree is balanced, the height is about log n, so those operations are O of log n, which is the whole point of a BST. But here's the catch I always raise: if I insert already-sorted data into a naive BST, every new value goes to one side, and the tree degenerates into what's essentially a linked list with height n, so operations become O of n. That's exactly why self-balancing trees like AVL and red-black trees exist, they keep the height logarithmic. And one elegant property: an inorder traversal of a valid BST always produces the values in sorted order, which is both a neat consequence and a simple way to check validity.

question: How do you find the height of a binary tree recursively?
title: Height of Binary Tree Java | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: The **height** of a binary tree is the number of edges (or nodes, by convention) on the **longest path from the root to a leaf**. Compute it recursively: a node's height is **1 + max(height(left), height(right))**, with an empty subtree returning **0** (or -1 for edge-count). It's **O(n)** time and **O(h)** stack space - a clean post-order recursion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can write the post-order recursion and define the base case consistently
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Inconsistent base case (node-count vs edge-count), or computing depth top-down incorrectly
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State the recurrence 1 + max(left, right) and the O(n)/O(h) complexity, noting node vs edge convention

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Height = longest **root-to-leaf** path.
- Recurrence: **`1 + max(left, right)`**; base `null -> 0`.
- **Post-order** (need children first).
- **O(n)** time, **O(h)** stack space.
- Be explicit about **node vs edge** counting convention.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The height of a binary tree is the length of the longest path from the root down to a leaf. There are two common conventions, counting nodes on that path or counting edges, and I just make sure to pick one and be consistent. With the node convention, an empty tree has height zero and a single node has height one. The recursive solution is very clean, and it's naturally a post-order recursion, because to compute a node's height I first need to know the heights of both of its subtrees. So for any node, I recursively compute the height of its left subtree and the height of its right subtree, and then the node's height is one plus the maximum of those two. The base case is an empty subtree, a null node, which returns zero under the node convention, or minus one if I'm counting edges. The one plus accounts for the current node itself, and forgetting it is a classic off-by-one error. This visits every node exactly once, so it's O of n time, and it uses O of h stack space, where h is the height, because that's how deep the recursion goes. One thing I'd note is that for a badly skewed tree, where the height approaches n, that recursion depth could risk a stack overflow on very large inputs, in which case I'd consider an iterative approach. The same max-of-the-two-subtrees recurrence is the foundation for related problems like computing a tree's diameter or checking whether it's height-balanced.

sections.title: Tree Height with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Inconsistent base case**: node-count returns 0 for null; edge-count returns -1. Don't mix them.
- **Top-down depth confusion**: height is naturally **bottom-up** (post-order); don't conflate with root-down depth.
- **Off-by-one**: forgetting the `1 +` for the current node.
- **Deep/skewed trees**: recursion is **O(h)** stack; a skewed tree (h=n) can risk stack overflow.

question: How does level-order traversal (BFS) work on a binary tree?
title: Level Order Traversal BFS Binary Tree | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **Level-order traversal** visits nodes **level by level**, top to bottom, left to right - it's **BFS** on a tree. Use a **queue**: enqueue the root, then repeatedly dequeue a node, process it, and enqueue its non-null children. To group output by level, record the **queue size** at the start of each level and process exactly that many nodes. **O(n)** time, **O(w)** space (w = max width).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you implement BFS with a queue and know the level-size trick to group by level
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to do level-order with recursion (that's DFS), or not capturing level boundaries
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the 'snapshot queue size per level' technique and give O(w) space (widest level)

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Level-order = **BFS** on a tree; uses a **queue**.
- Enqueue root, dequeue + enqueue children each step.
- **Snapshot `q.size()`** per level to group output.
- **O(n)** time, **O(w)** space (max width).
- Recursion gives DFS, not level-order.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Level-order traversal visits the tree one level at a time, from the top down, and left to right within each level. It's really just breadth-first search applied to a tree, and the key tool is a queue, not recursion, because recursion naturally produces a depth-first order instead. The basic algorithm is: enqueue the root, then loop while the queue isn't empty, dequeuing a node, processing it, and enqueuing its non-null children. That alone gives you the nodes in level order. But very often the interviewer wants the output grouped by level, as a list of lists, and that's where the nice trick comes in. At the start of each iteration of the outer loop, I take a snapshot of the current queue size, call it k. Because of how BFS works, those k nodes currently in the queue are exactly the nodes on the current level. So I process precisely k nodes, collecting their values into one level's list and enqueuing their children, and when I've done all k, I've finished that level and I move on to the next. The time complexity is O of n, since every node is processed once. The space complexity is O of w, where w is the maximum width of the tree, the largest number of nodes on any single level, because that's the most the queue ever holds at once, and for a full tree that bottom level can be roughly half the nodes. The main mistakes to avoid are reaching for recursion, which gives DFS, and forgetting the level-size snapshot, without which you can't tell where one level ends and the next begins.

- **No level-size snapshot**: without capturing `q.size()` up front, you can't tell where one level ends.
- **Enqueuing nulls**: only enqueue non-null children, or guard before processing.
- **Wrong space estimate**: space is **O(w)** (widest level), which can be ~n/2 at the bottom.

question: What is the difference between a binary tree and a heap?
title: Binary Tree vs Heap Java | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: A **binary search tree** orders nodes left-smaller / right-larger for **O(log n) search** of any value. A **heap** is a **complete** binary tree satisfying only the **heap property** (parent <= children for a min-heap), giving **O(1) access to the min/max** but no efficient search for arbitrary values. Heaps are usually stored in an **array**; BSTs use linked nodes. Use a BST for ordered search, a heap for priority queues.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you distinguish the ordering guarantees: full ordering (BST) vs only parent-child (heap)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking a heap is sorted or supports fast search, or that a BST gives O(1) min
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note heaps are array-backed complete trees with O(1) peek, BSTs give O(log n) arbitrary search

sections.title: Binary Search Tree vs Heap
sections.content:
Both are binary trees, but their **ordering guarantees** differ fundamentally. A **BST** maintains a **total ordering**: for every node, the **entire left subtree is smaller** and the **right subtree larger**. This supports **O(log n) search** for *any* value (when balanced) and an inorder traversal gives sorted output.

A **heap** only guarantees the **heap property** between **parent and child**: in a **min-heap**, each parent is **<=** its children (max-heap: `>=`). There's **no ordering between siblings**, so you **cannot search** for an arbitrary value efficiently - but the **min (or max) is always at the root**, giving **O(1) peek** and **O(log n)** insert/extract. A heap is also a **complete** tree, which lets it be stored compactly in an **array** (children of `i` at `2i+1`, `2i+2`); BSTs use linked nodes.

sections.title: BST vs Heap
sections.content:
blue|BST|~total ordering|left < node < right|O(log n) search any value|inorder = sorted
emerald|Heap|~parent-child only|min/max at root|O(1) peek, O(log n) push/pop|no sibling order
amber|Heap structure|~complete tree|stored in an array|children at 2i+1, 2i+2|compact, cache-friendly
rose|Pick by need|~search vs priority|ordered search -> BST|priority queue -> heap|both O(log n) updates

sections.content:
| Aspect | BST | Heap |
|---|---|---|
| Ordering | Full (left<node<right) | Parent vs child only |
| Search arbitrary value | O(log n) balanced | O(n) - not supported |
| Get min/max | O(log n) (or O(h)) | **O(1)** at root |
| Insert / delete | O(log n) balanced | O(log n) |
| Storage | Linked nodes | Array (complete tree) |
| Typical use | Ordered lookups, ranges | Priority queue, top-K |

sections.title: Heap - O(1) min, but no value search
BST (TreeSet) - O(log n) ordered search
When to Use Each
sections.content:
- **BST (TreeMap/TreeSet)**: ordered lookups, range queries (`ceiling`/`floor`/`subSet`), sorted iteration, searching arbitrary values.
- **Heap (PriorityQueue)**: priority queues, scheduling by priority, repeatedly extracting the min/max, **top-K** problems, Dijkstra/Prim.
- If you only ever need the smallest/largest repeatedly, a heap is simpler and faster than a BST.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **BST**: full ordering -> **O(log n) search** of any value; inorder sorted.
- **Heap**: only parent <= children -> **O(1) min/max**, no value search.
- Heap is a **complete** tree stored in an **array**.
- Both: insert/delete **O(log n)**.
- BST for **search/ranges**; heap for **priority queues/top-K**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Both are binary trees, but the difference is in how strongly they're ordered. A binary search tree maintains a full ordering: for every node, the entire left subtree is smaller and the entire right subtree is larger. That total order is what lets you search for any value in O of log n when the tree is balanced, and it's why an inorder traversal of a BST gives you the values sorted. A heap is much weaker in its ordering. It only guarantees the heap property between a parent and its children, so in a min-heap every parent is less than or equal to its children, and in a max-heap it's the reverse. Crucially, there's no ordering between siblings or across the tree, which means a heap cannot search for an arbitrary value efficiently, that's O of n. What a heap does give you is the minimum, or maximum, always sitting right at the root, so peeking at it is O of one, and inserting or extracting is O of log n. There's also a structural difference: a heap is a complete binary tree, which means it can be stored compactly in an array, where the children of index i are at two i plus one and two i plus two, making it cache-friendly. A BST is normally built from linked nodes. So I choose based on what I need. If I need to search for values or do range queries, I use a BST, which in Java is TreeMap or TreeSet. If I need a priority queue, repeatedly pulling the smallest or largest element, like in top-K problems or Dijkstra's algorithm, I use a heap, which in Java is PriorityQueue.
